entities.summary:
Citibank (Citigroup Inc.) is one of the world's largest financial institutions, founded in 1812 as the City Bank of New York, becoming the first US bank to issue credit cards (1950 Diners Club partnership), first bank with an ATM network (1977), and one of the most globally interconnected banks in history. At its 2007 peak, Citigroup was the world's largest bank by assets, but its catastrophic exposure to subprime mortgage securities during the 2008 financial crisis required a $45 billion US government bailout.

Citibank's history parallels American finance: founded by city merchants, it financed the US Civil War, helped fund the Erie Canal, and by the 1920s was America's largest bank. John Reed and Walter Wriston transformed Citibank in the 1970s-1980s through credit card innovations (including the Citi card's move to South Dakota to escape New York usury limits) and aggressive global expansion. Sandy Weill's 1998 merger of Citicorp with Travelers Group creating Citigroup was the largest corporate merger in history at the time, requiring repeal of the Glass-Steagall Act.

The 2008 crisis exposed Citigroup's overexposure to collateralized debt obligations: the bank lost $27.7 billion in 2008 alone and required three separate government bailouts totaling $45 billion. The US government owned 27% of Citigroup stock during the crisis period. Citigroup's near-collapse demonstrated the 'too big to fail' problem and directly influenced the Dodd-Frank financial reform legislation.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Citibank's 2008 near-collapse requiring $45 billion in government bailouts made it the defining emblem of 'too big to fail' financial institutions, and the credit card innovations it pioneered transformed global consumer banking.
